s: Article III extends judicial power only to "Cases" and "Controversies."
From the beginning the Justices declined to give the executive legal advice.
In 1793, Chief Justice Jay politely refused Secretary of State Jefferson's request for guidance on neutrality questions.
Hayburn's Case (1792) involved circuit-riding Justices refusing to serve as pension commissioners whose decisions the Secretary of War could revise.
It established that federal court judgments cannot be subject to revision by the political branches.
That principle was reaffirmed in Plaut v. Spendthrift Farm (1995), which barred Congress from reopening final judgments.
A justiciable controversy requires (1) actual adverse parties, (2) a real dispute rather than a hypothetical, and (3) a likelihood that the court's decision will have practical legal effect.
Declaratory judgments are permissible when they resolve an actual controversy between parties with adverse legal interests.
